title: Latency‑Aware Selective Verification in Generate–Validate NetOps Pipelines: A Preregistered Paired Study with gpt‑5‑mini
abstract: We preregistered (CAND‑2026‑001) and executed a paired, artifact‑backed study that evaluates whether inserting a selective, low‑latency verification tier (risk scoring + fast validator) into an LLM→generate–validate–repair NetOps pipeline reduces unsafe commits while meeting a latency SLO. Using a deterministic synthetic intent corpus (N=400 paired intents, 10% deterministic adversarial variants), gpt‑5‑mini as generator, and a deterministic full‑checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) as ground truth, we observed baseline valid proposals = 399/400 (0.9975) and guarded valid proposals = 400/400 (1.000). Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired‑bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0075] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The preregistered latency hypothesis (H2) is unresolved because per‑stage latency telemetry required by the preregistration was not archived. All raw responses, per‑episode scorer JSONs, validator traces, provider‑call logs, model configuration, and analysis artifacts are archived with SHA‑256 hashes and file paths (see Disclosure Statement) to enable deterministic reproduction and inspection.

sections.introduction:
Automation that maps operator intent to concrete device configuration promises large productivity gains for network operations, but safety and latency are fundamental operational constraints: incorrect automated proposals can cause outages, while heavyweight verification can exceed operational SLOs. Recent work demonstrates generate–validate–repair pipelines and tool‑augmented LLM agents for NetOps; however, the operational trade‑off between safety gain and verification latency remains understudied. We ask the preregistered research question (CAND‑2026‑001): Can a selective, low‑latency verification tier (risk scoring + fast validator) integrated into a generate–validate–repair pipeline reduce unsafe commits versus LLM‑only while meeting a preregistered end‑to‑end latency SLO?
Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired experiment (N=400) with complete artifact provenance (responses, scorer JSONs, validator traces, provider calls, model configuration, and analysis artifacts) enabling deterministic replay. (2) An empirical safety result under the shared‑initial candidate protocol: baseline 399/400, guarded 400/400 (paired difference 0.0025; exact McNemar p=1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap CI [0.0,0.0075]; bootstrap resamples=10,000, seed=1729). (3) Transparent disclosure of a preregistered latency hypothesis that could not be evaluated because required per‑stage timing telemetry was not archived; we document where telemetry was expected and the absence in the archived manifest.
sections.related_work: This study builds on two converging lines: LLM‑driven NetOps (intent→configuration, repair) and verifier‑augmented LLM pipelines. Prior benchmarks and tool‑augmented agent studies (e.g., Cornetto and agentic repair evaluations) emphasize that verification plus iterative repair improves correctness but add latency and cost; other works integrate digital twins and formal validators for stronger guarantees. Unlike broad leaderboards, our contribution is a preregistered, paired design that isolates the verifier effect (given the same generated candidate) and publishes deterministic artifacts for inspection and replay. Representative nearby works used for positioning are archived with this run (manuscript evidence bundle cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration. We froze a detailed machine‑readable preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001) before execution. The preregistration specifies the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), confirmatory hypotheses H1 (safety) and H2 (latency SLO), sampling plan (N=400 paired intents with deterministic 10% adversarial variants), retry/missingness rules, analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), and exact bootstrap parameters (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). The preregistration identifier and binding provenance are recorded in the execution manifest and disclosure. Implementation artifacts referenced below are archived with SHA‑256s.
Corpus and generator. The confirmatory corpus is a deterministic synthetic operator‑intent generator (400 unique intents; 40 deterministic adversarial variants). Declared generator: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). To control generator variance and isolate verifier/repair effects we preregistered independent_condition_generation=false, delivering the same shared_initial candidate to both conditions (shared‑initial protocol).
Conditions and validators. Two conditions were compared per intent (paired): baseline = LLM‑only acceptance judged by the ground‑truth validator; guarded = LLM candidate evaluated by a selective (risk scoring + fast validator) tier before acceptance. Ground truth / full checker = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (archives: per‑episode JSON scoring records include validator traces; see execution/scoring/*.json). The validator performs deterministic per‑command parsing, dependency checks, and final intent constraint validation and emits a binary valid/invalid label plus structured trace.
Scoring and analysis. Primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided applied to the paired contingency (n11,n10,n01,n00). The contingency and all per‑episode scorer JSONs are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256: a6906bb4..., per‑episode scorer JSONs under execution/scoring/*.json). Confidence interval: paired bootstrap (percentile) with 10,000 resamples and seed=1729. The analysis executor and its log are archived (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256: 9ea0d56d...). Deterministic reconciliation of model call accounting (planned vs actual) is archived (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA‑256: a7570bf6...). All raw responses and provider calls are archived for replay (execution/responses/*.txt, execution/provider_calls/*.json).
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The run completed the preregistered confirmatory set: completed_episode_count = 800 (400 pairs), model_calls_used = 401 (shared_initial_generation=400 + repair=1), maximum_model_calls allowed = 800; the reconciliation artifact documents these counts (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json; sha‑256 a7570bf6...).
Safety (H1, preregistered). Per archived scoring JSONs and the contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256: a6906bb43712dcf82b3bc8bdc0ef095d228bcdc8a6a857d9cbbba1ad87245af8): n11=399 (both conditions valid), n10=1 (guarded valid, baseline invalid), n01=0 (baseline valid, guarded invalid), n00=0 (both invalid). Thus baseline valid proposals = 399/400 = 0.9975, guarded valid = 400/400 = 1.000, paired estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025.
Exact McNemar (two‑sided). We applied the archived exact_mcnemar_two_sided implementation in paired_binary_analysis_v1 to discordant counts (n10=1,n01=0); the executor returned p = 1.0 for the two‑sided test. (Why p=1.0? With extremely small discordant counts and the exact two‑sided definition realized by the archived implementation, the probability mass of the observed minimal discordance under the null yields a two‑sided p that equals 1.0 when the only discordant outcome is in one direction with count=1 and its symmetric counterpart is zero; the analysis executor and its parameters are archived so readers can reproduce the exact test behavior: analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (SHA‑256: 9ea0d56d...).) Paired bootstrap (percentile) CI = [0.0, 0.0075] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729).
Representative evidence and inspectability. The single discordant pair is archived for direct inspection: execution/scoring/task-000149-baseline.json (SHA‑256: fe147f43e33432ed446d76500c2c9566ca5f72086abbacb5ee84b13774a9d18e) and execution/scoring/task-000149-guarded.json (SHA‑256: d0cbfe9a4181cd87f35c9ead5b6697e1adcfde23e52461e8c21e5219fe607ca3). These per‑episode JSON files include the normalized candidate, raw candidate hash, validator trace (parsed commands, violations, final state), and provider‑call references so the reader can deterministically replay why baseline was marked invalid while guarded accepted the candidate. Key analysis artifacts necessary to reproduce the primary numerical claims are archived and hashed: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (a6906bb4...), analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (9ea0d56d...), analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json (a7570bf6...), execution/model_configuration.json (a40e96e2...), and the full execution manifest with provider‑call hashes.
Latency (H2) status. The preregistration required per‑stage end‑to‑end timing telemetry (generation start/stop, risk scoring start/stop, fast validator start/stop, full checker start/stop). Those timing fields were not archived in the confirmatory artifact bundle (execution manifest and analysis logs record their absence). Consequently we cannot evaluate H2 (95th‑percentile latency ≤ 2000 ms) from the supplied artifacts and therefore make no latency claim. The absence of the telemetry is documented in execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json.
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation. The observed absolute safety gain is small because the generator produced near‑ceiling valid candidates under the deterministic validator: baseline 0.9975; guarded 1.0. The bootstrap CI includes zero; exact McNemar p=1.0 results from the archived exact two‑sided implementation applied to discordant counts (n10=1,n01=0). Practically, when generator baseline is near ceiling, marginal verifier benefits on this estimand will be small; in lower baseline or adversarial regimes the verifier could deliver larger absolute safety gains. The preregistration included exploratory scans (verification threshold sweeps, subgroup analyses over adversarial items) and these raw scored artifacts permit such post‑hoc investigation; all per‑intent scoring JSONs are archived.
Shared‑initial design implications. We intentionally preregistered independent_condition_generation=false (a shared_initial candidate to both conditions) to isolate verifier/repair contributions. This produces a conditional estimand: the verifier effect given the specific generated candidate set. This choice reduces variance attributable to generator sampling but alters interpretation relative to an independent‑generation estimand (joint generator+verifier effect). The reconciliation artifact documents the accounting consequence: model_calls_used=401 rather than the 800 calls that would arise under independent generation counting (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json; SHA‑256: a7570bf6...). Both estimands are operationally meaningful but answer different managerial questions; practitioners should choose the estimand aligned with the operational decision.
Limitations and threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared‑initial protocol controls generator variance but conditions the estimand on the observed candidate set; archived reconciliation and provider logs show no undisclosed reruns. Construct validity: the deterministic validator models operational safety constraints at an abstract level; its fidelity to specific vendor devices or production digital twins is a modeling assumption. External validity: single model (gpt‑5‑mini), synthetic corpus, and a single deterministic verifier limit generalization; artifacts permit follow‑up runs across models/validators. Conclusion validity: very small discordant counts produce wide uncertainty; the archived paired contingency and bootstrap parameters allow exact replication.
Operational implications. Under this preregistered setting, selective low‑latency verification produced a deterministically traceable but numerically small safety gain because the generator already produced near‑valid candidates for our synthetic intents. For operational deployment, decision makers should evaluate (a) generator baseline quality on their real intent distribution, (b) the fast verifier's false‑negative profile on OOD/adversarial intents (we included 10% deterministic adversarial variants), and (c) the latency budget with per‑stage telemetry (which must be archived in future confirmatory runs).
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, deterministically reproducible paired experiment that tested a selective low‑latency verifier in an LLM→NetOps generate–validate pipeline. The guarded intervention produced a small absolute safety improvement over an already‑high baseline; the effect is artifact‑traceable and reproducible from the archived files. The preregistered latency hypothesis (H2) could not be evaluated because required per‑stage timing telemetry was not archived; we fully disclose that absence and point to where telemetry was expected. All principal numeric claims, the single discordant example, model configuration, provider‑call traces, per‑episode scorer JSONs, and analysis artifacts are archived with SHA‑256 hashes to permit deterministic replay and independent verification. Future confirmatory work should (1) archive per‑stage latency telemetry to enable H2 evaluation, (2) evaluate broader model and validator ensembles, and (3) consider independent generation designs when the joint generator+verifier estimand is of operational interest.

disclosure_statement:
Disclosure Statement (mandatory, artifact‑backed):
- Initial master prompt (immutable archived reference): provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The Research Director selected the topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps) and approved pre‑lock constraints. After the autonomy lock the autonomous system performed literature review, study selection, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, and revision without manual post‑lock editing of technical content.
- Preregistration: Study ID CAND‑2026‑001 (frozen prior to execution). Preregistered elements included: primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), confirmatory hypotheses H1 (safety) and H2 (latency SLO), sampling plan (N=400 paired intents, 10% deterministic adversarial variants), shared_initial protocol (independent_condition_generation=false), retry/missingness rules, analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), and bootstrap parameters (resamples=10,000, seed=1729). Preregistration integrity is recorded in the execution manifest (preregistration_sha256: 086d248e89636e99e788232e78a99b63459648545e6e79ed763c29521f8f8572).
- Models, adapter, and orchestration: Declared generator = gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). Adapter/orchestration family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Provider family recorded in the execution manifest (execution/provider_calls/...). All model calls and provider traces are archived under execution/provider_calls/*.json with SHA‑256s in the execution manifest.
- Datasets, validators, and artifacts: Confirmatory corpus = deterministic synthetic intent generator (400 unique intents; 40 deterministic adversarial variants) produced under the preregistration. Ground‑truth verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5; per‑episode scoring JSONs are stored at execution/scoring/*.json (examples and SHA‑256s in execution manifest). Key analysis artifacts archived: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA‑256: a6906bb43712dcf82b3bc8bdc0ef095d228bcdc8a6a857d9cbbba1ad87245af8), analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (SHA‑256: 9ea0d56d48a5cc7ff198d85d0a12c21536fab716c042bd5eb2033492eda5b18e), analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json (SHA‑256: a7570bf6ff3a946e8397f02452ab846c82d5184b7768f006bd06359a1b177de7), execution/model_configuration.json (sha‑256 a40e96e2...), execution/scoring/task-000149-baseline.json (SHA‑256: fe147f43e33432ed446d76500c2c9566ca5f72086abbacb5ee84b13774a9d18e), execution/scoring/task-000149-guarded.json (SHA‑256: d0cbfe9a4181cd87f35c9ead5b6697e1adcfde23e52461e8c21e5219fe607ca3). These artifact paths and SHA‑256s are included so readers may deterministically inspect the single discordant example that underpins the numerical claim.
- Human involvement and autonomy boundary: Humans contributed pre‑lock infrastructure development, selection of the topic family, and approval of preregistration constraints. After the autonomy lock the autonomous principal researcher performed literature review, study selection, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, internal AI peer review, and revisions. No human manually edited technical manuscript content after the autonomy lock. All deviations, retries, and failures are logged in the execution manifest. The autonomy boundary and pre‑lock/post‑lock separation are documented in provenance/master_prompt.txt and the preregistration.
- Missing archived telemetry: The preregistration required per‑stage latency telemetry to evaluate H2 (generation, risk scoring, fast verifier, full checker timestamps). Those telemetry fields were not archived in the confirmatory artifact bundle; the absence is recorded in the execution manifest and analysis reconciliation. Consequently H2 is unresolved for this run; we do not make any latency claims.
- Reproducibility: All principal outputs (responses, per‑episode scorer JSONs, provider calls, task manifests, model configuration, analysis artifacts and logs) are archived with SHA‑256 hashes in the execution manifest to allow deterministic reproduction and independent inspection.
limitations: Synthetic deterministic corpus and single model (gpt‑5‑mini): external validity to heterogeneous real operator intents and other LLMs is limited.
Single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5): validator fidelity versus real device semantics/digital twin is an abstraction assumption.

Shared‑initial design (independent_condition_generation=false) yields a conditional estimand (verifier effect given the same generated candidate) rather than the joint generator+verifier estimand; model_calls_used=401 vs planned 800 is reconciled in analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json (SHA‑256: a7570bf6...).
Latency hypothesis (H2) could not be evaluated because per‑stage timing telemetry required by the preregistration was not archived; no latency claims are made for this run.
